newsitem.title: FINLAND: Pohjola rejig not seen fully priced in.
newsitem.headline: Pohjola rejig not seen fully priced in.

text.p: A plan by Finnish insurer Pohjola to take over mutual Suomi's life insurance arm is expected to get the go-ahead at a trustees' meeting next week, but analysts say that is not yet fully priced in the stock.

When Pohjola announced the planned reshuffle in February, its stock quickly rose to 140 markka, peaking at 158; it has since fallen to around 138 markka, partly on general market weakness but also on uncertainty about the plan, analysts said.
"A 'yes' is to a certain extent in the price, but there is also uncertainty," said Christian Kock at brokers Evli.

Pohjola wants to ride a boom in life-insurance but has not been able to since it is associated through cross-ownerships with life-insurer Suomi -- which officials say does not have enough solvency capital on its own to fund strong growth.
Pohjola has said it plans to buy Suomi's Salama corporate life-insurance unit and incorporate it into a new life insurance arm which would start selling corporate and private policies.
According to the plan, the rest of Suomi's insurance portfolio and assets would be transferred later, but Suomi would immediately stop selling new policies.

The scheme has been criticised, with some commentators saying the transfer of assets is unfair to current policy holders. Some members of Suomi's board of trustees, due to decide on the plan on Tuesday, have opposed it.
"Should they not approve the plan, (Pohjola's) share will probably fall," said Opstock analyst Jukka Linden; he also saw some upside if it wins approval.

Non-life insurance tends to grow slowly, which the industry says makes it difficult to create shareholder value through price gains. But a Nordic-wide boom in life-insurance has created an opportunity for stock prices to rise.
Many of the deal's details are still open, including what price Pohjola would pay for corporate life unit Salama: it named UK financial sector consultant Fox, Pitt & Kelton to advise.
Pohjola aims to start operating in life as one entity from July 1, but has not yet won the approval it needs from the authorities to transfer the insurance portfolios or set up a new life subsidiary.
It believes such approval is due to it by law, and that even though it expects a solution, it is prepared to go to the Supreme Administrative Court to win it.
"They are making a mess, it is a real nuisance ... but I guess there will be a solution (out of court)," one senior Pohjola official has said.

Another open issue is the timetable for the transfer of the rest of Suomi's insurance portfolio and assets, which Pohjola feels is not urgent and should happen within a couple of years, officials say.

And it is not clear what will happen to Suomi's 39 percent voting stake in Pohjola. Daily Helsingin Sanomat on Wednesday said they cannot be annulled and might be sold. But Pohjola sources say all the options are still being examined.
Pohjola says its current slower-growth non-life operation has surplus solvency. It wants to transfer some of this to the new life unit.
Its 6.43 billion markka total solvency capital at end-1996 was 2.5 times liabilities.
Of this, the surplus in Pohjola non-life is in the region of three billion markka, officials say, but some of this would be consumed in paying for Salama.

At end-1996, Suomi had about 4.03 billion markka in solvency capital -- 0.9 billion of this in Salama -- and the bulk of this, some 3.2 billion, is valuation items which fluctuate with asset values, like shares.

Pohjola officials say a 10 percent move in share prices either way from the end-1996 level would have a 569 million markka impact on Suomi's solvency capital. A one percentage point move in interest rates would have a 267 million impact.
